title: Ohio Jobs Program Wants Its Money Back After Company’s Failure to Deliver GMO Salmon
author: Anna Clark
content:
When a biotech company named AquaBounty Technologies announced plans to farm
genetically engineered Atlantic salmon at a new plant in Ohio, local and state
officials eagerly provided it with incentives. Not long after, the company
paused construction and auctioned off “new” and “unused” equipment. Now, the
state’s private economic development arm wants its $1 million back.

JobsOhio has requested repayment from AquaBounty by Sunday, according to a
company filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing also
notes that, at the end of September, AquaBounty was down to three employees
and $122,255 in cash.

AquaBounty said that its salmon could thrive in indoor freshwater farms and
help feed the world. Announced in 2021, the new development in Pioneer, Ohio,
was supposed to be its first large-scale production facility.

The project came with promises of 112 new jobs, plus more resources for
schools and infrastructure. It was believed to be the largest investment ever
in rural Williams County.

But AquaBounty, which had never made a profit over its 30 years in business,
faced a tangle of regulatory challenges and pushback from environmentalists.

Locals were also suspicious of how the village mayor’s personal interests were
tied up in the project. Among other moves, Pioneer Mayor Ed Kidston bought
land that AquaBounty wanted to build on. He then sold it to the company for
$1.5 million more than he’d paid.

AquaBounty’s plan was unproven, but, [as ProPublica reported last
year](https://www.propublica.org/article/aquabounty-pioneer-ohio-gmo-salmon-
fish), the company was buoyed by state and local resources — including the
million-dollar grant from JobsOhio. The company received the money in August
2021, according to financial filings, shortly after the project went public.

“Why the state was so eager to promote this industry is really puzzling,” said
Sherry Fleming of Williams County Alliance, a grassroots environmental group.
While AquaBounty had genetic engineering know-how, she said it seemed to have
limited experience in production.

“Why the state was so eager to promote this industry is really puzzling.” Nick
Hagen for ProPublica

In response to ProPublica’s queries, a press contact for AquaBounty said it
shares what it can in its SEC releases and filings, and that it’s still in
discussion with JobsOhio over the repayment demand. AquaBounty’s filing said
that "there can be no assurance that JobsOhio will agree to any payment
schedule or other accommodation.”

“Any collection or legal action by JobsOhio could result in additional costs
and management distraction,” it added.

Kidston didn’t respond to requests for comment. He said at the time that his
actions involving the plant were intended only to help the community. The
village administrator referred ProPublica to AquaBounty and its website.

JobsOhio operates privately but has a funding mechanism set up by the state
and a board appointed by the governor. Matt Englehart, a spokesperson for
JobsOhio, said in an email to ProPublica that it “operates with transparency
and accountability,” but its limited disclosures have  long been a sore point
for Ohioans.

On its website, JobsOhio says its funding model for specialized grants is
“independent” and accommodating of “unique needs.” Qualifications include, but
aren’t limited to, “job creation, additional payroll, fixed-asset investment
commitment, project return on investment, and project location.”

The AquaBounty grant depended on not only the creation of jobs, but also $222
million in capital investment and a payroll of more than $5.4 million by the
end of 2026. It had to maintain those commitments through the end of 2028.

Less than two years after it got the money, construction stalled. Roughly 30%
built, the site languished at the end of Kexon Drive, a smooth new road that
Pioneer had extended for its benefit.

AquaBounty sold equipment intended for the Ohio farm in 2024 and 2025. It also
sold its intellectual property for genetically engineered salmon. By the end
of September, according to its filing, its primary remaining assets were
unsold equipment, the land in Pioneer and the incomplete build.

JobsOhio and other economic development boosters should “take a good look at
this because they’re putting taxpayer dollars at risk when they advertise to
bring these industries in, and they haven’t done their homework to protect the
community,” Fleming said.

Englehart told ProPublica that he can’t discuss a situation that may result in
litigation. But with any company, he said, “when metric commitments are not
met, we work closely with those businesses” to help them overcome challenges.

If all options are exhausted, he added, “we will claw back some or all of our
dollars so they can be used for future economic development projects to
benefit Ohioans.”

JobsOhio’s demand notice came in September, the financial filing said,
informing the company that its equipment sales and consideration of
acquisition offers for the Ohio farm were a breach of the grant agreement.

AquaBounty “provided additional information” to JobsOhio in October, the
filing said, but the agency upheld its demand and requested repayment this
month. If it doesn’t come, the filing said, JobsOhio may refer the matter for
collections and “pursue the remedies available” under the grant agreement.

With an onerous process and uncertain outcomes, it’s “pretty rare” for
JobsOhio to try to claw back money, said Kristan Wong Karinen, a research
analyst with the nonprofit Good Jobs First, which tracks public subsidies in
economic development. More commonly, she said, it and other agencies will
renegotiate the contract — extending the time period for a company to meet
commitments, perhaps, or lowering requirements.

“In this case, with AquaBounty,” Wong Karinen said, “because they haven’t done
anything, they haven’t fulfilled any of the requirements, I feel like JobsOhio
is being forced into this.”
